unsupported_claims: The claim that the maps platform confirms replies are a ranking factor is unsupported. Its guidance says replies show customers that their feedback is valued, not that replies affect ranking.
Source [8] is not in the research notes and cannot be verified against them. The 68% survey figure is supported by [7] alone.
The notes support a statistically significant increase in listing calls, not an increase in bookings or revenue.
factual_concerns: The draft reports 17% more calls; the study found 7% more.
The 0.4-position ranking difference was not statistically significant. Omitting this materially overstates the evidence for a ranking improvement.
The assigned clinics replied to every new review, not necessarily every review.
missing_perspectives: The main study does not establish that replies improved rankings, but its non-significant result also does not prove there was no effect.
A 2025 pilot found a 0.9-position gain, but lacked random assignment. A separate auto-repair study found no ranking difference; its relevance to dental clinics is limited.
suggested_revisions: State the conclusion directly: the randomized study found a 0.4-position relative gain, but it was not statistically significant.
Correct 17% to 7%, and identify the call difference as statistically significant. Do not imply that bookings or revenue increased.
Replace the platform ranking-factor claim with its actual customer-feedback guidance, citing the platform source.
Remove source [8] and cite [7] alone for the practitioner survey. Describe the survey as opinion, not evidence of a ranking effect.
Change 'every review' to 'every new review' and briefly note the limitations of the pilot and agency case study.

unsupported_claims: The study assigned clinics to reply to every new review, not necessarily every review.
The notes report more calls, but do not establish more bookings or revenue; 'business benefit' should be qualified accordingly.
factual_concerns: The 11% increase in new reviews is reported, but its statistical significance is not specified. Avoid implying that it was a statistically established effect.
The nonsignificant ranking difference does not prove that replies have no ranking effect.
missing_perspectives: Platform guidance says replies show customers their feedback is valued; it does not claim a ranking benefit.
A 2025 pilot found a 0.9-position gain, but had only 20 clinics and no random assignment.
suggested_revisions: Change 'every review' to 'every new review.'
State that calls were 7% higher and statistically significant, while 11% more new reviews were observed without a reported significance test.
Conclude that the study found no statistically significant ranking improvement, rather than ruling out an effect.
Add a brief note on the platform guidance and, if space permits, the weaker 2025 pilot.

unsupported_claims: “The maps platform confirms that replies are a ranking factor” is unsupported and directly contradicts the notes: the platform says replies show customers their feedback is valued, but does not say they affect rankings.
Citation [8] (Local ranking factors survey 2026) is not among the research notes, so its support cannot be assessed.
Calling the findings a “business benefit” is broader than the notes establish; they report more calls and reviews, not overall business outcomes.
factual_concerns: The report says replying clinics received 17% more calls; the study notes say 7% more.
It presents the 0.4-position gain without noting that the difference was not statistically significant, which makes the ranking result sound more conclusive than it is.
The 11% increase in new reviews is stated as a definite effect without clarifying that the notes report a group difference but do not say it was statistically significant.
missing_perspectives: The platform guidance is important context and should be accurately summarized rather than described as confirming a ranking factor.

The report omits the 2025 pilot's 0.9-position gain and its lack of random assignment, as well as the auto-repair study that found no ranking difference. Both provide relevant context for the mixed evidence.
It omits that the randomized study measured rankings daily from 40 grid points across the county; this methodology helps readers assess the main result.
suggested_revisions: Revise the lead to say the reply group gained 0.4 positions relative to the comparison group, a difference that was not statistically significant; avoid implying a demonstrated ranking improvement.
Correct “17% more calls” to “7% more calls” and note that this difference was statistically significant.
Replace the platform claim with: “The platform says replies show customers that businesses value their feedback, but does not say replies affect rankings.”
Describe the review-volume result as an observed 11% difference, without implying statistical significance unless supported by a source.
Remove citation [8] unless its source and findings are verified, and briefly note the mixed context from the nonrandom 2025 pilot and the auto-repair study.

unsupported_claims: Calling the findings a “business benefit” goes beyond the reported outcomes: the notes establish more listing calls and reviews, not more bookings, revenue, or profit.
factual_concerns: “Replying did have measurable effects” may imply the 11% increase in new reviews was statistically significant; the notes do not report its statistical significance. Distinguish that observed difference from the statistically significant 7% increase in calls.
missing_perspectives: The report omits the 2025 pilot’s 0.9-position gain, while noting that it lacked random assignment—useful context for the mixed ranking evidence.
It omits the separate auto-repair study, which found no ranking difference, and platform guidance, which describes customer-facing value but does not say replies affect rankings.
suggested_revisions: Replace “a business benefit” with a narrower conclusion, such as “The study found more listing calls and new reviews, but no clear ranking benefit”; avoid implying bookings or revenue gains.
Clarify that the 7% call difference was statistically significant, while the notes do not specify significance for the 11% review-volume difference.
Add a brief note on the nonrandomized 2025 pilot and the auto-repair study to reflect the broader, mixed evidence; mention that platform guidance does not identify replies as a ranking factor.

unsupported_claims: The audit does not attribute most of the decline to the shorter return window, or to any single cause.
The 52% figure applies to surveyed shoppers who returned apparel, not necessarily to all returns.
Source [7] is not in the research notes; its support for the May–December comparison cannot be verified from them.
factual_concerns: The 2025 apparel return rate was 27.1%, not 21.7%; the rate fell by 3.3 percentage points.
As of November 18, 2026, a full-year 2026 audit and a May–December 2026 comparison include future dates. Their timing or status needs clarification.
The FitRight and policy comparisons show associations, not proof that either change caused the observed differences.
missing_perspectives: The audit measures items returned divided by items sold, includes exchanges, and counts items returned within 90 days; the FitRight evaluation describes orders.
The 2024 apparel return rate was 26.4%, providing useful context for the 2025 increase and 2026 decline.
The survey also found that 18% of respondents who returned apparel cited the item looking different from its photos.
suggested_revisions: Correct the opening to 27.1% in 2025 and a 3.3-percentage-point decline to 23.8% in 2026.
Replace the causal claim with a statement that the audit does not determine the causes. Present the tool and policy comparisons as potentially relevant but not causal evidence.
Clarify the survey denominator and that $11.40 is an average processing cost; add the audit methodology.
Remove or verify source [7], and resolve the apparent future-dated full-year and May–December figures before publication.

unsupported_claims: The survey found that 52% of shoppers who returned apparel cited wrong size as their main reason; it did not establish that wrong size caused 52% of returns.
The tool was used on 14% of online apparel orders, not necessarily 14% of all orders.
factual_concerns: As of November 18, 2026, the draft treats full-year 2026 figures and the May–December comparison as completed results. The notes do not explain whether these include estimates or future data.
The sizing-tool comparison and the timing of the policy change do not establish that either caused the decline. The draft should make that limitation explicit.
missing_perspectives: The overall decline was 3.3 percentage points. The audit counts items returned within 90 days divided by items sold and includes exchanges; the sizing-tool figures concern orders.
The audit’s 90-day counting period and the shorter 30-day return window are different measures. The notes do not establish how the policy change affected the audited rate.
suggested_revisions: Verify the reporting periods and data maturity before presenting 2026 and May–December results as final.
Rewrite the survey sentence as: ‘Among shoppers who returned apparel, 52% cited wrong size as the main reason.’
Specify ‘14% of online apparel orders’ and add that the tool comparison and policy timing are associations, not proven causes.
State the 3.3-percentage-point decline and briefly describe the audit denominator, 90-day window and treatment of exchanges.

unsupported_claims: The claim that the cap took cars off inbound roads is unsupported. Traffic fell 1.2%, but the roads department says the counts cannot establish why.
Source [8] is not in the research notes and does not support the Corwick comparison on the evidence provided.
factual_concerns: Weekday journeys rose 9.6%, not 6.9%, in March–August 2026 compared with the same months in 2025.
Extra trips are free only after a rider reaches the daily or weekly cap; the draft’s wording could imply they are always free.
The 18.0% increase measures unlinked trips, not journeys or unique riders. Increased transfers help explain the difference, but the figures do not establish how much of the increase the cap caused.
missing_perspectives: Among riders who reported traveling more, 27% named a new job or office return as their main reason, compared with 41% naming the cap. The survey does not establish the cap’s overall causal effect.
Corwick’s 2.3% increase was mostly attributed to office returns. Its comparison with Halden is suggestive, not a controlled estimate of the cap’s effect.
Weekend journeys rose 3.1%, and 2024 weekday journeys were 2.0% below 2025 levels, providing additional context on patterns and prior growth.
Journeys are estimated by linking tap-ins within 60 minutes; this methodological detail qualifies the headline measure.
suggested_revisions: Correct the headline increase to 9.6% and specify the March–August 2026 comparison with the same months in 2025.
Define unlinked trips and explain that the city’s 18% claim uses that measure, while the audit’s journey measure rose 9.6%. State that further trips are free after the relevant cap is reached.
Replace the traffic causation claim with the 1.2% decline and the roads department’s caveat, citing the traffic-count source.
Add the survey’s 27% finding and qualify both the survey and Corwick comparison as evidence consistent with multiple influences, not proof of causation.
Remove source [8] and cite [5] alone for Corwick; add the audit methodology and other contextual sources where used.

unsupported_claims: The draft does not explicitly claim the cap caused the entire 9.6% rise, but it should avoid inviting that inference: the before-and-after comparison alone does not establish causation.
factual_concerns: “Once extra trips were free” could imply that all additional trips or transfers were free. They became free only after a rider reached the daily or weekly cap.
The survey figure applies to riders who said they had travelled more since March, not to all riders or to a measured share of the ridership increase.
missing_perspectives: The survey also found that 27% of riders travelling more named a new job or office return as their main reason; Corwick’s increase was mostly attributed to office returns.
Weekday journeys were already higher in 2025 than in 2024, and weekend journeys rose 3.1% in 2026. These provide context but do not establish what caused the weekday change.
Journeys are estimates from tap-in data linked within 60 minutes, an important qualification to the headline measure.
Inbound road traffic fell 1.2%, but the counts cannot establish why; they do not demonstrate a shift from cars to the Metro.
suggested_revisions: State that the 9.6% rise is a year-over-year association, not an estimate of the cap’s causal effect. Describe Corwick as context, not a definitive counterfactual.
Clarify that further trips were free only after the applicable cap was reached.
Add the survey’s 27% job-or-office-return figure and qualify both survey percentages as self-reported reasons among riders who said they travelled more.
Add a brief note on the journey-estimation method and specify that the revenue comparison covers March–August 2026 versus the same months in 2025.

unsupported_claims: “The shorter return window caused most of the decline” is unsupported: the audit does not attribute the decline to one cause, and the 4.1-point comparison does not establish causation.
The report does not support describing the sizing tool as a cause of the overall decline. Its lower rate is for tool-used orders, which were only 14% of 2026 online apparel orders.
factual_concerns: The 2025 rate is misstated as 21.7%; the audit reports 27.1%.

“Orders … were returned 19.2% of the time” may imply an order-level rate. The audit defines its return rate as items returned divided by items sold; specify the measure and denominator where possible.
Source [7] is not among the research notes, and its cited summary is not substantiated by them.
missing_perspectives: The 2024 apparel rate was 26.4%, which would give useful context for the 2025–2026 change.
Footwear moved in the opposite direction: its rate rose from 17.9% to 18.5%.
Rates varied by region: 21.0% in the north versus 25.9% in the south.
Clarify that the audit counts items returned within 90 days and counts exchanges as returns; this is relevant when discussing a policy change from a 60-day to a 30-day window.
suggested_revisions: Correct the opening comparison to 23.8% in 2026, down from 27.1% in 2025.

Replace the causal claim about the shorter window with a qualified statement: after the April change, May–December rates were 4.1 percentage points lower than in the same months of 2025, but the evidence does not establish that the change caused the decline.
Present the FitRight figures as an association in the pilot—19.2% versus 25.6% for comparable orders—and note the tool's 14% usage; do not infer its contribution to the overall decline.
Describe the survey finding as applying to shoppers who returned apparel, and retain the $11.40 processing cost as context rather than evidence about why rates changed.
Use only sources listed in the notes, and add the audit's return-rate definition and relevant context if space permits.

unsupported_claims: “Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns” changes the survey’s denominator: the notes say 52% of shoppers who returned apparel named wrong size as their main reason, not that 52% of returns were for that reason.
factual_concerns: “Each return cost an average of $11.40” can sound like a fixed cost; the source gives an average processing cost per online apparel return.

The report gives the rate figures without the audit’s definition: it is items returned divided by items sold, with exchanges counted as returns, and counts items returned within 90 days. This matters when interpreting the shortened policy window.
missing_perspectives: The report should make clear that the evidence does not establish how much either the sizing tool or the policy change caused the 3.3-point annual decline. The tool covered only 14% of orders, and the notes do not establish a causal evaluation.

The policy comparison is important context: returns were 4.1 points lower from May to December after the window shortened from 60 to 30 days. The report should note this is an observed before/after difference, not proof of the policy’s effect; the shorter eligibility window may affect measured returns.
The survey also found that 18% of returning shoppers cited the item looking different from photos, another reported reason relevant to why apparel was returned.
The 2024 rate of 26.4% would help show the longer trend: the rate rose to 27.1% in 2025 before falling in 2026.
suggested_revisions: Change the survey sentence to: “Among shoppers who returned apparel, 52% named wrong size as their main reason; 18% cited the item looking different from the photos.”
Add the audit definition and clarify that exchanges count as returns; describe $11.40 as the average processing cost per return.

Add a sentence stating that the tool and policy changes coincided with the decline, but the available evidence does not isolate either change’s causal contribution. Note that the tool covered 14% of orders and the policy comparison is observational.
Optionally add the 2024 rate for context, while keeping the central comparison—23.8% in 2026 versus 27.1% in 2025—clear.

unsupported_claims: “The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads” claims a cause the traffic-count source explicitly says it cannot establish. It only reports traffic was 1.2% lower than a year earlier.
The draft says transfers explain part of the 18.0% rise in unlinked trips, but the notes do not quantify how much of that rise is due to more transfers versus more journeys.
factual_concerns: Weekday journeys rose 9.6%, not 6.9%, compared with the same months of 2025.
“Once extra trips were free” is too broad: additional trips are free only after a rider reaches the daily or weekly cap.
The references include an unprovided source [8] at a different URL from the comparison source in the notes. The listed city press release [3] is not used in the text.
missing_perspectives: The survey also found 27% of riders who said they travel more cited a new job or office return; this is relevant context for attributing the change to the cap.
Corwick’s 2.3% increase was mostly attributed to office returns, which complicates its use as a comparison.
Weekend journeys rose 3.1%, and 2024 weekday journeys were 2.0% below 2025 levels; these provide useful context for the weekday trend.
The report should distinguish the 9.6% increase in linked journeys from the 18.0% increase in unlinked trips, which count transfers separately. The city’s 18% claim uses the latter measure.
suggested_revisions: Correct the first paragraph to say average weekday journeys rose 9.6% versus the same months of 2025.
Explain that unlinked trips rose 18.0%, while transfers per journey increased from 1.4 to 1.6; avoid implying the notes establish how much transfers account for the unlinked-trip increase.
Replace the claim that the cap took cars off roads with the measured 1.2% traffic decline and the caveat that the counts cannot identify its cause.
Add the survey’s 27% office-return/new-job response and note that Corwick’s increase was mostly attributed to office returns.
Remove the unsupported [8] reference, and either use [3] to clarify the city’s unlinked-trip figure or remove it from the source list.

unsupported_claims: “Unlinked trips … rose 18.0%, partly because transfers per journey rose” implies a quantified explanation of the 18% increase. The notes show transfers rose, but do not measure how much of the increase that explains.
factual_concerns: “Once extra trips were free” is imprecise: further trips are free only after a rider reaches the daily or weekly cap.
missing_perspectives: The survey also found 27% of riders who said they travel more cited a new job or office return; this is important context alongside the 41% naming the cap.
The 2024 baseline says weekday journeys were 2.0% below 2025, useful context for interpreting the year-over-year increase.
Weekend journeys rose 3.1%, a useful comparison with the weekday change.
Car traffic was down 1.2%, but the roads department says the counts cannot establish why; this could be noted as context, not evidence that the fare cap shifted drivers to transit.
The report should clarify that these before-and-after figures, the Corwick comparison, and rider survey responses do not by themselves isolate the fare cap’s causal effect.
suggested_revisions: Qualify the transfer explanation: say transfers per journey increased, which could contribute to the difference between journey and unlinked-trip counts, but the notes do not quantify its contribution.
Describe the survey denominator precisely (“among riders who said they travel more”) and include the 27% who cited a new job or office return.
Add the 2024 baseline and weekend comparison, or explain why they are omitted.
Add a brief caveat that Corwick’s 2.3% increase and the survey responses provide context, not a controlled estimate of the fare cap’s effect; include the traffic-count caveat if discussing car use.

unsupported_claims: 'the maps platform confirms that replies are a ranking factor' — the platform help page says replies show customers you value feedback and explicitly does not say replies affect ranking. This claim is fabricated and inverts the source.

Citation [8] 'Local ranking factors survey 2026' (seosurvey-report.example/factors) does not appear in the research notes; it is cited for the 68% figure, which comes only from the practitioner survey [7].
factual_concerns: Calls figure is misstated: notes say 7% more calls, not 17%.
The 0.4-position gain is reported without noting it was not statistically significant. Presenting it bare implies a real ranking effect, and this answers the core question wrongly.

The conclusion framing ('evidence here shows a business benefit, and the maps platform confirms...') overstates. The defensible conclusion is that there is no significant ranking effect, alongside a significant 7% call lift.
missing_perspectives: No direct answer to the brief. Per the randomized study, replying did not significantly improve map-pack rankings in 2026.
Auto repair study (80 shops) found no ranking difference, which corroborates the null result.
The 2025 pilot (20 clinics, 0.9 gain, non-random) is omitted. Mention it as weaker, non-randomized evidence superseded by the 2026 RCT.
Methodology strengths are missing: random assignment and daily rank measurement from 40 grid points. These support trusting the null result over the agency claim.
Median reply time of 19 hours is omitted. This is minor context on how replying was implemented.
Review-volume (11%) significance is not stated in the notes; the report should not imply it was significant.
suggested_revisions: Rewrite the opening: 'Clinics randomly assigned to reply moved up 0.4 positions on average, a difference that was not statistically significant, so the study found no reliable ranking improvement.'
Change 17% to 7% and note that this difference was statistically significant.
Delete 'the maps platform confirms that replies are a ranking factor'. Replace with: 'The platform's guidance frames replies as customer communication and does not say they affect ranking.'
Remove citation [8], or replace it with a source that is in the notes.
Add the auto-repair null result and the 2025 non-random pilot, explaining why the RCT outweighs the pilot and the agency's 9-client uncontrolled claim.
Frame the 68% practitioner belief as a contrast with the evidence, not as support for it.

unsupported_claims: 'Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere' groups the 11% review-volume gain with the 7% call gain. The notes report statistical significance only for calls; no significance is given for review volume, so calling it a measurable effect overstates it.
factual_concerns: The 7% call increase is the only outcome the notes mark as statistically significant, but the draft does not say so. That leaves it on the same evidential footing as the unqualified 11% review figure.

'The evidence here shows a business benefit, not a clear ranking benefit' is reasonable. However, a non-significant 0.4-position difference means the study could not detect a ranking effect, not that it ruled one out. The notes give no confidence interval or power figure, so the draft should not imply there is no effect.
missing_perspectives: The platform help page frames replies as showing customers you value their feedback and does not say they affect ranking. This directly bears on the question and is omitted.

The 2025 pilot (20 clinics) found a 0.9-position gain but had no random assignment. It should be mentioned alongside the agency claim as weaker, non-randomized evidence that the 2026 randomized study did not replicate at that size.
The auto repair study (80 shops) found no ranking difference from replying, which is consistent with the null ranking result in another industry. It is omitted.
Methodology detail is missing: rankings were measured daily from 40 grid points across the county. This strengthens the null result.
The reply-speed context (median 19 hours) is missing. Readers cannot tell what reply practice was actually tested.

There is no discussion of possible indirect effects: higher review volume could plausibly affect rankings over a longer horizon. The study covered only six months, a limitation worth noting without speculating beyond the notes.
suggested_revisions: Change 'Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere' to state that clinics that replied got 7% more calls (statistically significant) and collected 11% more new reviews, with no significance reported for the review figure.
Add a sentence citing the platform guidance: it presents replies as customer-facing and does not claim a ranking effect.
Add the 2025 pilot (0.9 positions, 20 clinics, no random assignment) and the auto repair null result (80 shops) to give a fuller evidence picture.
Mention the daily 40-grid-point measurement and the 19-hour median reply time when describing the study.

Reword the conclusion along these lines: 'In the one randomized 2026 study, replying produced no statistically significant ranking change over six months, though it significantly increased calls; a small ranking effect cannot be ruled out.'
Add a source entry for each newly cited note: platform guidance, 2025 pilot, other verticals, reply speed.

unsupported_claims: 'The shorter return window caused most of the decline [1]' is not supported. The audit [1] explicitly does not attribute the decline to any single cause, so the citation contradicts the claim it is attached to.
Citation [7] (corvane-summary.example/audit-2026) does not appear in the research notes. The 4.1pp claim should cite only [4].
'each return cost an average of $11.40' overgeneralizes. The source specifies online apparel returns in 2026.
factual_concerns: The 2025 figure is wrong. The notes give 27.1%, not 21.7%. As written, 23.8% would be a rise, which contradicts the word 'down'. The correct change is a 3.3 percentage point decline.

The 4.1pp May–Dec drop is a year-on-year comparison that coincides with the window change. It also partly overlaps FitRight adoption and other factors, so it does not isolate the effect of the policy.

Shortening the window from 60 to 30 days may mechanically reduce counted returns. The audit counts returns within 90 days, so the policy limits what customers can return rather than changing what they want to return. This is not necessarily a fit or satisfaction improvement and should be noted.
The 52% wrong-size figure is a share of surveyed returners giving that as their main reason. It is not 52% of all returns as measured by the audit.
missing_perspectives: A rough attribution is missing. FitRight's effect on the overall rate is about 14% × 6.4pp ≈ 0.9pp, and that assumes the comparison is causal and the comparable orders are truly comparable. That is a small share of the 3.3pp drop.
The FitRight vendor claim of a 19% return rate covers only tool orders. Source [3] is listed but never discussed, and the report should warn that it should not be read as Corvane's overall rate.
Footwear returns rose slightly (17.9% to 18.5%), which is a useful contrast.
There is a large regional gap: 21.0% north versus 25.9% south.
18% of surveyed returners said the item looked different from the photos.
The audit methodology counts exchanges as returns, which matters for interpreting the rate and the sizing story.
The analyst expects a further decline in 2027 but gives no estimate, so this speculative claim should be labeled as such.
suggested_revisions: Correct the opening sentence to: 'down from 27.1% in 2025, a 3.3 percentage point decline [1].'

Delete 'The shorter return window caused most of the decline.' Replace it with: 'The audit does not attribute the decline to any single cause [1]; the timing is consistent with the April window change, but the evidence does not isolate its effect.'
Remove citation [7] and cite [4] for the 4.1pp figure.
Add the FitRight back-of-envelope estimate (about 0.9pp of overall impact), with caveats about the causality of the comparison.
Clarify that the 52% is the share of surveyed returners giving wrong size as their main reason, and add the 18% photo-mismatch figure.
Clarify that the $11.40 is the average 2026 cost of an online apparel return.
Add brief context: the 2024 rate, the footwear contrast, the regional gap, and that exchanges count as returns.
Either use [3] with a caveat that it covers only tool orders, or drop it from the source list.

unsupported_claims: 'Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns' misstates the survey. Source [5] says 52% of shoppers who returned apparel gave wrong size as their main reason. That is a share of respondents, not of returned items, and it comes from a self-reported third-party survey, not the audit.
factual_concerns: The draft presents the FitRight tool as a co-explanation without sizing its effect. The 6.4 pp gap on 14% of orders implies roughly 0.9 pp at most of the 3.3 pp overall decline, and less if tool users differ from non-users. The draft leaves readers to infer a larger role.

The audit counts returns made within 90 days. Cutting the window from 60 to 30 days therefore mechanically removes late returns from the count. Part of the decline may reflect fewer permitted returns rather than fewer unwanted items, and the draft does not say this.
The 4.1 pp May–Dec drop is not purely a policy effect. It also includes any tool effect and other changes in that period, so the two causes overlap and cannot simply be added together.

The May–Dec drop (4.1 pp) is larger than the full-year drop (3.3 pp). This implies January–April fell much less or rose. That supports the policy change as the bigger factor, but the draft does not point it out.
missing_perspectives: The 2024 baseline is omitted: the rate was 26.4% in 2024. The 2025 figure of 27.1% may have been elevated, so the 2026 fall partly reverses a rise.
Footwear returns rose from 17.9% to 18.5%. That rise is a useful contrast for judging whether company-wide factors drove the apparel drop.
Exchanges are counted as returns in the audit methodology. This affects how to interpret the rate and the cost figure.
The regional spread (21.0% north vs 25.9% south) is omitted. It suggests that composition or regional factors matter.
The analyst forecast of further declines in 2027 is omitted. It is speculative and gives no estimate, so if included it should be labeled that way.
suggested_revisions: Add an explicit attribution estimate. Tool: about 0.9 pp upper bound (0.14 × 6.4). Policy change: likely the larger driver, partly a mechanical counting effect. The two effects overlap.
Reword the survey sentence to: 'In a shopper survey, 52% of Corvane customers who returned apparel cited wrong size as the main reason, and 18% said items looked different from photos.'
Add a sentence on the 2024 rate (26.4%) and on footwear rising to 18.5% for context.
Note that exchanges count as returns.
Either connect the $11.40 cost to the analysis or drop it, since it does not address the 'why' question.

unsupported_claims: The claim that the maps platform confirms replies are a ranking factor is unsupported. Its guidance says replies show customers their feedback is valued, not that replies affect ranking.
Source [8], 'Local ranking factors survey 2026,' is absent from the research notes and cannot support the report.
'The evidence here shows a business benefit' is too broad: the notes establish more listing calls and reviews, not increased bookings, revenue, or profitability.
factual_concerns: The call increase was 7%, not 17%; the notes identify that 7% difference as statistically significant.
The report omits that the 0.4-position ranking difference was not statistically significant. Presenting the gain without this qualification misleadingly suggests an established ranking improvement.
The intervention was replying to every new review, not necessarily every review.
missing_perspectives: The report needs a direct answer: the January–June 2026 randomized study did not establish that replying improved rankings. A nonsignificant result also does not prove there is no effect.
The 2025 pilot found a 0.9-position gain but lacked random assignment; this is weaker supporting evidence worth distinguishing from the larger randomized study.
The separate study of 80 auto repair shops found no ranking difference. This provides context, though it is not direct evidence about dental clinics.
Practitioner belief is opinion evidence, not a demonstration of ranking effects.
suggested_revisions: Revise the opening to: 'In a randomized study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics from January to June 2026, clinics assigned to reply to every new review gained 0.4 map-pack positions relative to controls, but the difference was not statistically significant.'
Replace '17% more calls' with '7% more calls, a statistically significant difference'; retain the 11% review increase without implying its statistical significance was established.

Replace the conclusion with: 'Replying was associated with more listing calls and new reviews, but the study did not establish a ranking improvement. Platform guidance encourages replies as a customer-service practice and does not state that they affect ranking.'
Remove source [8], cite the supplied platform guidance, and briefly contextualize the weaker pilot and agency findings alongside the null result in auto repair shops.
Limit conclusions to the January–June study period rather than implying evidence covering all of 2026.

unsupported_claims: “Reply to every review” broadens the intervention beyond the notes, which specify replying to every new review.
factual_concerns: “Measurable effects elsewhere” groups the 7% call increase and 11% review increase without distinguishing statistical support: only the call increase is explicitly reported as statistically significant.
“A business benefit” is broader than the measured outcomes. The notes show more listing calls and new reviews, not increased bookings, revenue, or profit.
missing_perspectives: The platform guidance endorses replies as a customer-feedback practice but makes no claim that replies affect ranking.
The 2025 pilot found a 0.9-position gain but lacked random assignment; this is relevant weaker positive evidence.
The separate study of 80 auto repair shops found no ranking difference, although its applicability to dental clinics is limited.
The draft does not explicitly distinguish a statistically nonsignificant finding from proof that replies have no ranking effect, or limit its conclusion to January–June 2026.
suggested_revisions: Change “reply to every review” to “reply to every new review.”

Write: “Replying clinics received 7% more listing calls, a statistically significant difference, and collected 11% more new reviews; the notes do not report statistical significance for the review-volume difference.”
Conclude: “The randomized study did not establish a ranking benefit during January–June 2026, although it does not rule out an effect. It did find a significant increase in listing calls.”
Add a brief context sentence covering the weaker positive pilot, the null auto-repair finding, and the platform guidance, while keeping the randomized dental study central.

unsupported_claims: 'The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads' has no citation, and the notes contradict it: the roads department says the 1.2% drop in counts cannot show what caused the change.

Source [8] 'Regional transit comparison 2026' (regiontransit-data.example) does not appear in the research notes. Only regiontransit.example/compare-2026 is listed, so [8] looks fabricated or mismatched.

'Partly because transfers per journey rose' is cited as support from the audit [2], but the audit does not explain the gap. Only [4] gives the transfer figures. The arithmetic also suggests transfers explain most of the gap, not just part of it: 1.096 × 1.6/1.4 ≈ 1.25, which is broadly consistent with the 18% gap.
factual_concerns: The weekday journey growth is misstated as 6.9%. The audit says 9.6%, so the digits are transposed. This is the headline number.
Fare revenue fell 6.2% only for March to August 2026 versus the same months of 2025. The draft drops this time frame.
The 41% survey figure covers only riders who said they travel more. The draft omits that 27% named a new job or office return, which overstates how clearly the survey points to the cap.
missing_perspectives: The draft never mentions the city press release [3] claiming an 18% weekday ridership rise. It does not explain that this figure counts unlinked trips and so overstates growth compared with 9.6% in journeys. This is central to the 'what changed' question.

There is no counterfactual reasoning. Corwick rose 2.3%, mostly from office returns, so roughly 7 points of Halden's 9.6% may be attributable to the cap. Even that is uncertain because Corwick is only one comparison city.
The 2024 baseline is missing. Weekday journeys were already growing about 2% a year (2024 was 2.0% below 2025), which suggests some pre-existing trend.
Weekend journeys rose only 3.1%. This contrast with weekdays is relevant to the 'why' question and could reflect commuting and office returns, or a different effect of the weekly cap.
The draft does not define journeys versus unlinked trips. Journeys are linked from tap-ins within 60 minutes.
suggested_revisions: Correct 6.9% to 9.6% and state that the comparison is the same months of 2025.
Add a sentence contrasting the city's 18% claim (unlinked trips) with the audit's 9.6% (journeys), and cite [3].
Delete or rewrite the car traffic claim: 'Inbound car traffic was 1.2% lower, but the roads department says the counts cannot show the cause.' Add a source entry for the traffic counts.
Remove source [8], or replace it with the correct Corwick source, and cite only [5].

Add the 27% job or office-return survey figure, the 3.1% weekend figure, and the 2024 trend. Frame the cap as a likely but not sole driver, with an estimated effect of roughly 7 points above Corwick's trend, caveated.
Add 'March–August 2026 vs 2025' to the revenue sentence.

unsupported_claims: 'once extra trips were free' is broader than the notes. The transfer source says only that capped riders no longer pay per transfer. Rephrase to match: transfers rose because capped riders stopped paying per transfer.
factual_concerns: The draft never states plainly that the city's 18% headline overstates the change in weekday ridership. The comparable journey-based figure is 9.6%. Placing the two numbers side by side without a conclusion lets readers take 18% as the ridership effect.
The 18% claim is attributed to [3] alone, while the 18.0% figure comes from [2]. That is acceptable, but the wording should make clear that the city's 18% is the unlinked-trip count, not journeys.

The transfer explanation is plausible but unquantified. If transfers means additional boardings, 1.096 × (2.6/2.4) ≈ 1.19, which is consistent with the 18% unlinked-trip rise. If it means vehicles per journey, the implied rise is about 25%, which does not fit. The notes do not define the term, so 'partly' should stay hedged and the definition should be flagged as unclear.
The revenue figure covers March–August 2026 versus the same months of 2025. The draft drops that time frame.
missing_perspectives: Corwick's 2.3% rise was mostly attributed to office returns. The draft omits this, and it is the key context for using Corwick as a counterfactual: roughly 7 percentage points of Halden's gain exceed the no-cap comparison.

The survey's 27% who named a new job or office return is omitted. Citing only the 41% overstates the evidence. The survey is also limited to riders who report travelling more, and the answers are self-reported.
The 2024 baseline (weekday journeys 2.0% below 2025) points to a pre-existing upward trend of about 2% a year. Some of the 9.6% rise may have happened without the cap.
Weekend journeys rose only 3.1%, far less than weekdays. This is relevant to the why question: it suggests commuting or office-return effects, or that weekly caps bind mainly for weekday commuters.
Car traffic on main inbound roads fell 1.2%, but the roads department says the counts cannot show cause. This is weak evidence of mode shift and should carry that caveat.
Methodology is missing: journeys are estimated by linking tap-ins within 60 minutes, so the 9.6% figure is an estimate.
The report never directly answers the 'why' half of the brief. It needs a synthesis paragraph weighing the cap against office returns, trend growth, and transfer-counting effects.
suggested_revisions: Add an explicit statement: the comparable ridership measure is weekday journeys, up 9.6%; the city's 18% counts unlinked trips and overstates the increase in people travelling.
Expand the Corwick sentence: 'Corwick, with no cap, saw weekday journeys rise 2.3%, mostly attributed to office returns, suggesting background factors explain only part of Halden's 9.6%.'
Report both survey results (41% fare cap, 27% new job or office return) and note that they are self-reported by a subset of riders.
Add the 2024 baseline trend, the 3.1% weekend rise, and the 1.2% traffic decline with the roads department's caveat.

Add a short 'What explains the rise' section concluding that the evidence is consistent with the cap driving a substantial share of the increase, but not all of it, and that causation is not established.
Add sources for the weekend, 2024 baseline, traffic and methodology notes. Restore the March–August time frame for revenue.

unsupported_claims: "down from 21.7% in 2025" — the notes say the 2025 audited online apparel return rate was 27.1%, not 21.7%.

"The shorter return window caused most of the decline" — the notes show a 4.1 percentage-point lower rate from May–Dec 2026 versus the same months in 2025, but they do not establish that this caused most of the annual decline.

Citing [7] for the May–December comparison is unsupported because the provided notes do not include a separate summary source and the claim is already attributable to the return policy change notice in [4].
factual_concerns: The year-over-year change is misstated: 23.8% in 2026 versus 27.1% in 2025 is a 3.3 percentage-point decline, not a drop from 21.7%.
The report overstates causal certainty. The audit explicitly says it does not attribute the decline to any single cause.

The FitRight evidence is incomplete as written: 19.2% vs 25.6% is for comparable orders, but the tool covered only 14% of orders, so the report should not imply it explains the overall annual decline by itself.
The report omits the 2024 baseline (26.4%), which helps contextualize the longer-term trend.
The wording "wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns" is fine, but it should be clear this is among shoppers who returned apparel, not all shoppers or all orders.
missing_perspectives: The audit’s own limitation that it does not attribute the decline to any single cause.
The 2024 return rate (26.4%) to show multi-year movement.
The regional split: northern region 21.0% vs southern region 25.9%, which may indicate geographic variation in returns.
The possibility that the policy change and sizing tool both contributed, rather than one being the dominant driver.
The analyst note expecting further decline in 2027 as the sizing tool spreads, while noting it is only an analyst expectation with no estimate.
suggested_revisions: Correct the 2025 comparison to 27.1%, and state the decline was 3.3 percentage points year over year.
Replace "caused most of the decline" with a cautious formulation such as "likely contributed to the decline, alongside other factors" or "the evidence points to at least two contributors."
Add the audit caveat that it does not attribute the decline to any single cause.
Clarify that the FitRight 19.2% vs 25.6% comparison applies only to comparable orders and the tool was used on 14% of online apparel orders in 2026.
Add one sentence on the 2024 rate and/or the regional differences to give broader context.
If keeping the policy-change figure, cite only the return-policy source and avoid implying it explains the entire annual drop unless the report explicitly says the evidence does not isolate effects.

factual_concerns: The draft says the two changes 'coincided' with the decline, which is acceptable, but it still risks implying causation more strongly than the audit supports. The audit explicitly says it does not attribute the decline to any single cause.

'Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns' is true only for shoppers who returned apparel in 2026, not for all apparel returns in the category overall; the wording should make that population explicit.
The draft omits the 2024 apparel return rate (26.4%), which is relevant context for the 2026 change and shows the rate has been trending down before 2026.
missing_perspectives: The report does not mention that Corvane’s annual audit counts every item returned within 90 days and includes exchanges as returns, which matters for interpreting the headline return rate.
It omits the regional split showing materially different 2026 return rates in the north (21.0%) and south (25.9%), which could help explain variation beyond FitRight and policy changes.

It omits that Corvane’s own evaluation found 19.2% return rates for FitRight orders versus 25.6% for comparable non-tool orders, and that FitRight was used on only 14% of online apparel orders; this is important for judging how much the tool could have moved the overall rate.

It omits the evidence that return rates from May to December 2026 were 4.1 percentage points lower than in the same months of 2025 after the return-window change, which is the strongest available timing-based evidence for a policy effect.
It omits the footwear comparison, which rose slightly in 2026, and could serve as a partial counterpoint suggesting apparel-specific drivers rather than a broad companywide return decline.
It omits the analyst note that expects further decline in 2027 as the sizing tool spreads, though this is forecast rather than evidence.
suggested_revisions: Replace 'Two changes coincided with it' with more cautious wording such as 'The notes point to two plausible contributors, but the audit does not isolate a single cause.'
Add one sentence clarifying that the 19% FitRight figure is for tool orders only, and that Corvane's own pilot found 19.2% vs 25.6% for comparable orders without the tool.
Clarify that the 52% wrong-size figure comes from a shopper survey of returners, not all customers or all returns.
Add a brief context sentence with the 2024 apparel return rate (26.4%) and the audit method (returns within 90 days; exchanges counted as returns).
Consider adding the regional split and the footwear comparison to show that the apparel decline may reflect apparel-specific factors rather than a companywide returns shift.

unsupported_claims: "In the six months after the cap began, average weekday journeys rose 6.9% compared with a year earlier" — the notes say the audit found a 9.6% rise in average weekday journeys, not 6.9%.
"The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads" — the traffic counts only show car traffic was 1.2% lower; the notes explicitly say they cannot show what caused the change.

"Fare revenue fell 6.2%" — the notes say fare revenue from March to August 2026 was 6.2% lower than the same months of 2025, but the draft omits that this is revenue, not ridership, and does not make clear it is a separate outcome rather than evidence of causation.
factual_concerns: The key ridership figure is wrong: 9.6% weekday journeys increase in the audit, not 6.9%.

The draft underplays the distinction between linked/"journeys" and unlinked trips. The audit’s main weekday ridership figure is journeys; the 18.0% figure is for unlinked trips and should not be used as the headline ridership change.

"Partly because transfers per journey rose from 1.4 to 1.6 once extra trips were free" is plausible, but the notes support this as an explanation for more unlinked trips, not as the sole or fully established reason for the ridership increase.

The comparison to Corwick is presented without the context that Corwick’s 2.3% rise was mostly attributed to office returns; that makes it a limited control, not direct evidence that Halden’s extra growth was all due to the cap.
missing_perspectives: The draft omits the rider survey result that 27% of riders who said they travel more named a new job or office return as the main reason, which is important for explaining the increase.
It omits the audit finding that average weekday journeys were already 2.0% below 2025 levels in 2024, which could provide baseline context for the 2026 comparison.
It omits weekend ridership, which rose only 3.1%, suggesting the post-cap effect was stronger on weekdays than weekends.
It omits the city’s own press-release claim that weekday ridership increased 18%, which is a useful contrast with the audit’s 9.6% linked-journey figure and 18.0% unlinked-trip figure.
It omits that the city subsidized the revenue gap by 4.8 million, which is relevant to the policy tradeoff and may matter for interpreting the cap’s effects.
suggested_revisions: Replace "6.9%" with "9.6%" for the audit-based weekday journeys figure, and keep "18.0%" only for unlinked trips.

Revise the causation sentence to something like: "The evidence suggests the fare cap contributed to higher ridership, but survey responses also point to new jobs and office returns as another important factor."
Change "The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads" to "Main inbound road traffic was 1.2% lower than a year earlier, but the counts cannot show whether the fare cap caused the change."

Add a sentence distinguishing linked journeys from unlinked trips, e.g. "The audit’s 9.6% figure refers to journeys, while the city’s 18% claim counts unlinked trips and therefore includes transfers."
Add a brief balancing clause on Corwick: "Corwick rose 2.3% over the same period, mostly due to office returns, so some of Halden’s increase may reflect broader post-pandemic travel trends."
If mentioning revenue, specify that fare revenue fell 6.2% and the city covered the gap with a 4.8 million subsidy, but do not treat this as evidence that the cap caused the ridership increase.

factual_concerns: The draft implies the 18% unlinked-trip increase is directly attributable to transfers rising from 1.4 to 1.6. The notes support that transfers per journey increased after the cap, but they do not establish that this is the sole or even primary cause of the 18.0% unlinked-trip rise.

The comparison to Corwick is presented as if it meaningfully explains Halden’s change, but the notes only say Corwick saw a 2.3% rise, mostly attributed to office returns. They do not support using Corwick as a counterfactual or as evidence that the fare cap caused the remaining increase in Halden.

The draft states 'Among riders who travel more, 41% named the fare cap as the main reason' without clarifying that this is only a subset of surveyed riders, not all riders or all increased riders. As written, it may overstate how representative the survey result is.

The draft’s mention of fare revenue and subsidy is accurate but somewhat detached from the research question; it could be read as implying a direct link between ridership gains and the subsidy, which the notes do not establish.
missing_perspectives: The report omits weekend ridership, which rose only 3.1%, a useful contrast showing the fare-cap effect was stronger on weekdays.
It omits the baseline context from 2024 showing 2025 weekday journeys were already 2.0% above 2024, which matters for interpreting how much of the 2026 increase is incremental.
It omits the survey finding that 27% of riders who travel more cited a new job or office return, an important competing explanation for the weekday rise.
It omits the traffic-count evidence that main inbound road traffic was 1.2% lower year over year, which is suggestive but explicitly not causal.
It omits the note that the city’s 18% claim counts unlinked trips, which is central to explaining why the city’s number is larger than the audit’s 9.6% linked-journey figure.
suggested_revisions: Add a sentence distinguishing linked journeys (up 9.6%) from unlinked trips (up 18.0%) and explain that the city’s headline figure uses the latter.
Revise the transfer explanation to say the rise in transfers per journey is consistent with the unlinked-trip increase, not proof that it caused all of it.
Add the survey’s 27% 'new job or office return' result to present a fuller explanation of why ridership rose.
Add the 3.1% weekend increase and/or the 2024 baseline so readers can judge whether weekday growth was unusually strong.
Soften the Corwick comparison: say it provides context only, not a clean causal benchmark for the fare cap.

unsupported_claims: “The shorter return window caused most of the decline [1]” is unsupported. The audit explicitly does not attribute the decline to any single cause; the policy notice establishes timing and a year-over-year association, not causation or its share.
Source [7], https://corvane-summary.example/audit-2026, is absent from the research notes and cannot support the report.
factual_concerns: The 2025 audited apparel return rate was 27.1%, not 21.7%. The actual decline was 3.3 percentage points to 23.8%; the draft's figures instead imply an increase.
“Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns” changes the survey's denominator. The finding concerns 52% of surveyed shoppers who returned apparel, not necessarily 52% of returned items.

The notes cover May–December and full-year 2026 despite the current date being November 18, 2026. The report should flag this unresolved timing issue rather than present all figures as completed-period results.
missing_perspectives: The audit measures returned items divided by sold items, includes exchanges, and counts returns within 90 days across all online orders. This matters when comparing it with a shortened customer return window and order-based tool figures.

The report should explicitly distinguish FitRight's lower-return association from a proven causal effect. Comparable orders do not establish random assignment, and 14% adoption does not establish its contribution to the overall decline.
FitRight's promotional 19% figure applies only to tool-assisted orders, not Corvane's overall return rate; this scope distinction is important when evaluating competing figures.
The 2024 rate of 26.4% provides useful context: 2026 was below both 2025 and 2024, rather than necessarily continuing an established downward trend.
suggested_revisions: Replace the opening with: “Corvane's audited online apparel return rate fell 3.3 percentage points, from 27.1% in 2025 to 23.8% in 2026 [1]. The audit does not identify a single cause.”

Replace the causal assertion with: “The shorter return window coincided with lower reported returns, while tool-assisted orders also had lower return rates; the available evidence does not isolate either factor's causal contribution.”
Retain the pilot figures and limited adoption, but clarify that they concern tool-assisted versus comparable non-tool orders, not an experimentally established company-wide effect.
Describe the survey result as “52% of surveyed apparel returners cited wrong size as their main reason.”
Add a short audit-methodology note with its supplied source, remove unsupported source [7], and verify the reporting dates before treating full-year and May–December results as final.

unsupported_claims: “Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns” changes the survey denominator. The notes say 52% of surveyed shoppers who returned apparel named wrong size, not that 52% of returned items had that cause.
factual_concerns: As of November 18, 2026, full-year 2026 figures and a completed May–December comparison cannot be final historical results, particularly with 90-day return tracking. The notes themselves contain this timing problem; the report should flag it rather than silently present these periods as complete.
missing_perspectives: The report does not quantify the overall decline: 3.3 percentage points, or approximately 12.2% relative to 2025.

The audit measures returned items divided by items sold, includes exchanges, and tracks returns within 90 days. These definitions matter when comparing the audit with order-based tool figures and a shortened customer return window.
The tool comparison and the timing of the policy change do not establish causal contributions. The notes do not establish randomized tool adoption or isolate the policy change from other influences.
A shorter return window could lower recorded returns by restricting return eligibility, rather than by improving fit or satisfaction.
The survey also identifies appearance differing from photos as the main reason for 18% of returning shoppers, providing a relevant non-sizing explanation.
suggested_revisions: Add “a decline of 3.3 percentage points, approximately 12.2%” after the headline figures.
Replace the survey sentence with: “Among surveyed Corvane shoppers who returned apparel in 2026, 52% named wrong size as the main reason and 18% said the item looked different from the photos.”
Define the audit’s item-based denominator, inclusion of exchanges, and 90-day tracking period; avoid treating order-level tool usage as an item-level share.
State explicitly that the evidence is consistent with sizing assistance and tighter return eligibility contributing, but does not establish how much either caused the overall decline.
Verify the reporting dates and whether the 2026 figures are final, provisional, or forecasts before presenting full-year and May–December results as observed.

unsupported_claims: “The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads” asserts causation the notes explicitly do not establish. Traffic fell 1.2%, but the roads department says the counts cannot explain why.
Source [8], including its URL, is absent from the research notes and cannot support the Corwick comparison. Source [5] alone supports the reported 2.3% increase.
factual_concerns: The headline weekday-journey increase is wrong: the audit reports 9.6%, not 6.9%, for March–August 2026 versus the same months of 2025.
“Once extra trips were free” is too broad: further trips become free only after a rider reaches the daily or weekly cap.
missing_perspectives: Define journeys versus unlinked trips, and explicitly explain that the city's 18% ridership claim counts unlinked trips rather than origin-to-destination journeys.

Include competing explanations: 27% of surveyed riders who traveled more cited a new job or office return, and Corwick's 2.3% growth was mostly attributed to office returns. The evidence does not isolate the cap's causal effect.
The survey percentages apply only to riders reporting increased travel, not all riders, and are self-reported reasons rather than a causal estimate.
Weekend journeys rose only 3.1%; weekday journeys in 2024 were 2.0% below 2025 levels. These provide useful context on variation and pre-existing growth.
Journeys are estimated by linking tap-ins within 60 minutes, a relevant measurement limitation when transfer behavior changes.
suggested_revisions: Replace “rose 6.9%” with “rose 9.6% in March–August 2026 compared with March–August 2025.”
Explain that journeys count origin-to-destination travel regardless of transfers, while unlinked trips count each boarding separately; increased transfers partly explain the larger 18.0% rise.
Replace the car-causation sentence with: “Inbound car traffic fell 1.2% year on year, but the counts cannot establish whether the fare cap caused the decline.” Cite the traffic-count source.
Add the survey's 27% job/office-return result and Corwick's office-return explanation; conclude that the cap likely contributed, but its independent effect is not established.
Remove source [8], qualify free travel as occurring after the cap is reached, and specify that the revenue decline covers March–August versus the same period in 2025.

unsupported_claims: “Once extra trips were free” implies a blanket removal of marginal fares. The notes say further trips are free only after a rider reaches the daily or weekly cap.
factual_concerns: The draft correctly distinguishes the 9.6% rise in journeys from the 18.0% rise in unlinked trips, but should explicitly state that neither before-and-after increase establishes how much growth the cap caused.
The survey describes riders who said they travel more, not independently verified increases. Preserve that self-reported qualification.
missing_perspectives: Alternative explanations are underdeveloped: 27% of surveyed riders reporting increased travel named a new job or office return, and Corwick’s 2.3% growth was mostly attributed to office returns.

The survey supports the cap as a reported motivation, but its selected respondent group cannot establish the cap’s share of total ridership growth. Corwick is contextual evidence, not an established causal control.
The draft omits useful context: weekend journeys rose 3.1%, and 2024 weekday journeys were 2.0% below 2025 levels, indicating growth predated the cap.
The journey measure is an estimate based on tap-ins linked within 60 minutes; this matters to the central distinction between journeys and unlinked trips.
suggested_revisions: Specify the comparison as March–August 2026 versus March–August 2025, including for the revenue figures.
Replace “once extra trips were free” with “as capped riders no longer paid for additional transfers after reaching the cap.”
Add: “Among riders who said they travelled more, 41% cited the cap as their main reason and 27% cited a new job or office return. Corwick’s growth was mostly attributed to office returns.”
Add a clear conclusion: “The evidence suggests the cap contributed to increased travel, but does not isolate its causal effect from office returns or other changes.”
Briefly define journeys as origin-to-destination trips estimated by linking tap-ins within 60 minutes; add the weekend and earlier baseline comparisons if space permits.

unsupported_claims: "clinics randomly assigned to reply to every review" is only supported by the methodology note, not by the study summary cited in [1]; the draft should cite [2] directly for random assignment.
"Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere: clinics that replied received 17% more calls from their listings" is not supported by the notes; the source says 7% more calls, not 17%.

"the evidence here shows a business benefit" is broader than the reported ranking result and is only partially supported; the notes do show more calls and reviews, but the draft should avoid implying a strong overall causal business conclusion without qualification.
factual_concerns: The draft converts the statistically insignificant 0.4-position ranking difference into a straightforward positive result. The notes say the ranking difference was not statistically significant, so the wording should not imply a proven ranking lift.
The calls result is misstated as 17% instead of 7%.
The draft cites an additional source [8] that is not in the provided research notes, so that reference is unsupported in this review context.
Saying the platform 'confirms' ranking impact is overstated; the guidance is silent on ranking.
missing_perspectives: The draft omits that the ranking difference was not statistically significant, which is the key finding for the research question.
It omits the 2025 pilot with a 0.9-position gain, which provides prior but weaker evidence.
It omits the auto-repair study showing no ranking difference from replying, an important counter-example.
It omits the reply-speed detail (median 19 hours), which may be relevant context for interpreting the study.

suggested_revisions: Replace the opening sentence with: 'In a controlled study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics in the first half of 2026, clinics randomly assigned to reply to every review moved up 0.4 map-pack positions on average, but the difference was not statistically significant.'
Change 'received 17% more calls' to 'received 7% more calls' and, if desired, note that this difference was statistically significant.

Delete 'the maps platform confirms that replies are a ranking factor' and replace it with 'the platform's help page encourages replies as a customer-service practice but does not say they affect ranking.'
Remove or qualify 'the evidence here shows a business benefit' to specify the limited outcomes: more calls and more reviews, but no significant ranking improvement.
Either remove source [8] or replace it with a source that is actually in the notes; otherwise the citation list is not aligned with the provided evidence.

unsupported_claims: “Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere” is broader than the cited notes, which only show a statistically significant 7% increase in calls and 11% more new reviews in this specific study; they do not establish general effects elsewhere.

“the evidence here shows a business benefit” is a bit too broad if meant generally; the notes only support higher calls and review volume in this study, not an overall business benefit across outcomes.
factual_concerns: The draft says clinics were “randomly assigned,” but it omits that rankings were measured daily from 40 grid points, which matters for interpreting the ranking result and should be reflected if the summary is meant to be methodologically complete.
“In the first half of 2026” is accurate but less precise than the source, which specifies January to June 2026.

The phrase “moved up 0.4 map-pack positions relative to the others” could imply a meaningful improvement; the notes say the difference was not statistically significant, so the wording should avoid implying a real ranking effect.
missing_perspectives: The 2025 pilot with a 0.9-position gain is omitted; even if weaker evidence, it is relevant context for prior findings.
The other-industry study of 80 auto repair shops finding no ranking difference is omitted and provides an important counterexample.

suggested_revisions: Change the lead sentence to: “In a controlled randomized study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics from January to June 2026, clinics that replied to every new review averaged 0.4 positions higher in the map pack than non-repliers, but the difference was not statistically significant.”

unsupported_claims: The draft says 2025 return rate was 21.7%, but the research notes give 27.1% for 2025 from the audit; 21.7% has no support in the notes.

The claim that the shorter return window 'caused most of the decline' is stated as fact citing the audit, but the audit explicitly does not attribute the decline to any single cause; no source quantifies the window's share of the decline.

The 4.1 percentage point reduction from May to December is attributed to the return window change, but the notes give no causal attribution and the comparison period overlaps with the FitRight tool rollout.
Citation [7] (audit summary at corvane-summary.example) does not appear in the research notes; it is unverifiable from the provided material.

Citation [3] (FitRight customer story) is listed in sources but never cited in the text, and its 19% claim is not used; its omission is fine but the draft does not flag that this figure covers only tool orders and conflicts with the 19.2% pilot figure.

The claim that wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns is stated as 'of returns' generally, but the survey covers only shoppers who returned apparel and is a self-reported survey, not audited return data.
factual_concerns: The 2025 baseline is wrong: the notes say 27.1%, so the draft's implied change (down about 2.1 points) is incorrect; the actual decline is about 3.3 points.

The draft implies the 2026 decline is partly explained by two coinciding changes but never reconciles that the 2026 rate (23.8%) and the 2025 rate (27.1%) differ from the 2024 rate of 26.4%, which means 2025 rose before falling.

Presenting the FitRight pilot (19.2% vs 25.6%) alongside the overall decline implies the tool drove the drop, but the comparison is between self-selected orders, not randomized, and the tool covers only 14% of orders, so it can explain only a small part of the overall change.

The draft describes the 4.1-point gap as a return-rate change across May–December, but it does not state it is a comparison against 2025 under a different policy; it also does not give the level, so readers cannot judge scale.
Audit counts exchanges as returns and counts all items within 90 days; the draft does not mention this definition, which matters when comparing to the 60-to-30-day window change.
The footwear rate rose (17.9% to 18.5%) and the regional gap (21.0% north vs 25.9% south) are omitted; the footwear rise is relevant counter-evidence against a general policy-driven decline.
missing_perspectives: Footwear returns rose slightly while apparel fell, which the draft omits; this is relevant to whether the policy change or the sizing tool is the driver, since footwear was presumably not targeted the same way.
The FitRight vendor claim of 19% (tool orders only) and the company pilot's 19.2% are both tool-only figures and cannot be used to estimate the overall effect; the draft should say so.
No discussion of the analyst's view that the decline will continue as the sizing tool spreads, nor the caveat that it gives no estimate.
Regional differences (21.0% north vs 25.9% south) are unmentioned, so the draft cannot say whether the changes affected regions evenly.
Cost data ($11.40 per return) is given without the total volume or the cost change, so the economic significance is unclear.
No mention that the audit does not attribute the decline to any single cause, which is the central caveat for the 'why' question.
suggested_revisions: Correct the 2025 baseline to 27.1% and restate the change as a decline of about 3.3 percentage points.

Remove 'caused most of the decline'; replace with: the audit does not attribute the decline to a single cause; the return window shortening and the FitRight tool both coincided with it, and the notes do not separate their effects.
State that the 19.2% vs 25.6% pilot comparison is observational, covers 14% of orders, and cannot by itself account for the overall decline.
Drop or verify citation [7]; cite [3] only if the 19% vendor claim is discussed and flagged as covering tool orders only.
Qualify the 52% wrong-size figure as a self-reported survey of shoppers who returned apparel, not audited return data.
Add footwear and regional figures and state that the 'why' remains partly unresolved given the available evidence.

unsupported_claims: The draft says the two changes 'coincided with' the decline, which implies causal association the notes do not establish; the notes say the audit does not attribute the decline to any cause.

'Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of returns' overstates the survey: the notes say 52% of shoppers who returned apparel gave wrong size as the main reason, from a shopper survey (not the audit), so it is a self-reported share of respondents, not of returns.
'Each return cost an average of $11.40 to process' is stated without noting the notes define this as including shipping, inspection and restocking, and it is an average for 2026 only.
The draft's claim that the 4.1-point lower rate from May to December is attributable to the return window is not in the notes; the notes give only a comparison of months, with no attribution.
factual_concerns: The 4.1 percentage point figure compares May–December 2026 with the same months of 2025, but the audit's full-year decline is 3.3 points (27.1% to 23.8%) and covers all months including January–April, so the two figures are not reconciled and the draft does not explain the difference.

The draft's use of the 19.2% vs 25.6% comparison is presented as evidence about the tool's effect, but the notes describe it as Corvane's own evaluation of comparable orders; selection bias (tool users may differ) is not discussed.

Sources are labeled [1]-[6] but the draft's claim about 52% is attributed to a survey of shoppers who returned apparel, not to all returns; the heading phrasing is misleading.
missing_perspectives: The 2024 baseline (26.4%) and the 2025 figure (27.1%) are in the notes but the draft never places 2026 in multi-year context, so the trend (rising 2024→2025, falling 2025→2026) is omitted.

Shopper survey sample size, method and whether it covers Corvane shoppers only are not reported; the 18% 'looked different from photos' finding is omitted entirely.
suggested_revisions: Replace 'Two changes coincided with it' with explicit language that the audit does not attribute the decline, and that the sizing tool and the return window change are both plausible but untested contributors.

Quantify the sizing tool's possible contribution: 14% of orders at a 6.4-point gap implies roughly 0.9 points of overall effect if the comparison were causal; state this as a rough, assumption-dependent bound.
Remove or qualify the 52% sentence: 'Among shoppers surveyed who returned apparel, 52% named wrong size as the main reason (shopper survey, sample not reported).'
Add the 2024 and 2025 baselines and the footwear and regional figures to give context.
Add the methodology caveat (exchanges counted as returns; 90-day window) and note the 19% FitRight figure is not reconciled with the 19.2% pilot figure.

missing_perspectives: The 2025 pilot (0.9 gain, no random assignment) is omitted, and so is the reason it is weaker evidence than the randomized 2026 study.
