The platform guidance page is not cited, though it directly addresses whether replies affect ranking.
Reply speed (median 19 hours) and the measurement method (daily, 40 grid points) are not used; the method is a strength worth noting.
Possible causal link between more reviews or calls and ranking is not discussed, and the 6-month window limits conclusions about longer-term effects.
Limitations are not stated: the study is a single county and 60 clinics per arm may be underpowered to detect a small effect, so 'no significant difference' is not proof of zero effect.
suggested_revisions: Open with a direct answer: in the randomized 2026 study, replying was associated with a 0.4-position gain that was not statistically significant, so there is no reliable evidence that replies improved map-pack rankings.
Correct 17% to 7% for calls and note it was statistically significant.
Delete the claim that the platform confirms replies are a ranking factor; state that the platform's help page says replies show customers you value feedback and makes no ranking claim.
Remove citation [8] and cite only [7] for the 68% figure, labelling it as practitioner belief rather than evidence.
Add the 2025 pilot (non-randomized, 0.9) and the auto repair null result, and the platform guidance as a cited source.
Add a caveat that a non-significant result with n=60 per group cannot rule out a small effect, and that the data cover only Jan-June 2026 in one county.
Rewrite the final paragraph so the conclusion is that replying shows business benefits (more calls, more reviews) but not demonstrated ranking gains.

unsupported_claims: The draft says replying produced a "business benefit", which treats the calls result as established. The notes only report 7% more calls with no mention of bookings, revenue or patients. The source is titled "Calls and bookings" but gives no booking data.

The draft implies replying caused the 11% review-volume gain and the 7% call gain. The notes give no significance test for the review-volume figure, so "collected 11% more" is presented with more certainty than the notes support.
"Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere" is only partly supported. The ratings source shows no effect, and the volume figure has no stated significance.
factual_concerns: "Not a clear ranking benefit" understates the evidence. The study found a 0.4-position difference that was not statistically significant, which means no detectable effect, not a weak benefit. The draft should say a ranking effect was not detected and cannot be ruled out, given the study's power.

The draft says "the first half of 2026" for a study that ran January to June, which is fine, but it says nothing about the study's limits: 6 months, one county, and 120 clinics. Presenting it as a definitive answer is overstated.

The draft says "replied to every review" as the study treatment, but the notes say the replying group replied to every new review. The wording blurs this; it could imply replies to historical reviews.
The 3-position agency claim is dismissed briefly, but the draft does not say that it conflicts with the controlled results or that the agency has a commercial interest.
missing_perspectives: The 2025 pilot (20 clinics, 0.9-position gain, no random assignment) is omitted. It is relevant counter-evidence and should be mentioned with its limitations.
The auto repair study (80 shops, no ranking difference) is omitted. It is corroborating evidence from another vertical, though it may not generalize to dental clinics.
The platform guidance, which says replies show customers you value feedback and does not claim a ranking effect, is omitted. It supports the conclusion that replying is a customer-facing benefit.
The reply-speed data (median 19 hours) is omitted, and the report does not discuss whether faster replies matter.
The methodology (random assignment, daily measurement from 40 grid points) is cited but not described, so readers cannot judge the strength of the study.
The draft does not discuss statistical power, confidence intervals, or whether 0.4 positions would be practically meaningful if it were real.
suggested_revisions: Rewrite the conclusion: "A randomized study found no statistically significant ranking effect (0.4 positions); a small effect cannot be ruled out. Replies were associated with 7% more calls (significant) and 11% more reviews."
Replace "business benefit" with specific findings and note that the notes give no booking or revenue data.
Add the 2025 pilot and the auto repair study in one sentence each, with their limitations.
Add the platform guidance noting it makes no ranking claim.
Describe the methodology (random assignment, 40-grid-point daily tracking) when first citing the study, and cite [2] there.
Note that the 68% practitioner belief is opinion, not evidence of an effect.
Qualify the review-volume result by noting that no significance test is reported, and state that the study did not test whether the extra reviews would affect ranking over a longer period.

unsupported_claims: The draft says clinics that replied 'received 17% more calls'; the notes say 7% more calls, so this figure is unsupported.
The draft says 'the maps platform confirms that replies are a ranking factor'; the platform guidance explicitly does not say replies affect ranking.
Citation [8] 'Local ranking factors survey 2026' (seosurvey-report.example/factors) does not appear in the research notes and cannot be verified against them.
The draft says the 0.4-position gain was from clinics 'randomly assigned to reply to every review'; the notes say the 0.4 gain was not statistically significant, which the draft omits.
The draft implies the 68% practitioner belief is a meaningful signal; the notes give no evidence this belief is accurate.
factual_concerns: The 0.4-position result is presented as a finding without stating it was not statistically significant; this materially overstates the ranking evidence.
The 0.4 figure is described as moving 'up 0.4 map-pack positions relative to the others' without noting the study's direction or confidence interval; the reader cannot judge its size.
The 17% call figure contradicts the source (7%), an outright factual error.

The 2025 pilot (0.9-position gain, no random assignment) is omitted; it is the only other ranking-related evidence and should be cited with its limitations.

The draft mentions 'the first half of 2026' correctly but does not note that the study period was January to June and that the report is dated November 2026, so findings may need a note on whether they still hold.
missing_perspectives: Non-significance of the main ranking result: the draft should state plainly that the study found no statistically significant ranking effect.
The auto repair study (80 shops, no ranking difference) is a counter-signal across industries and is omitted.
The reply speed finding (median 19 hours) is omitted; it could matter for interpreting whether timely replies differ from slow ones.
Limitations of the agency claim: 9 clients, no comparison group, and a commercial interest in the result, should be stated explicitly.
Limitations of the main study's measurement: rankings from 40 grid points across the county, and whether the sample of 120 clinics generalizes beyond Brennick County.
The platform's own statement that replies show customers feedback is valued, which is a non-ranking benefit, should be presented as what the platform actually says.
suggested_revisions: Replace the 17% call figure with 7% and note it was statistically significant.

Remove the claim that the maps platform confirms replies are a ranking factor; state instead that platform guidance describes replies as showing customers their feedback is valued and does not say they affect rankings.

Rewrite the opening: 'In a randomized study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics (Jan–Jun 2026), clinics that replied to every review moved up 0.4 map-pack positions on average, a difference that was not statistically significant.'
Verify citation [8] against the research notes or remove it; the notes do not include it.
Add the 2025 pilot (0.9 gain, non-randomized, 20 clinics) and the auto repair null result as context on the strength and consistency of the evidence.

Drop or heavily qualify the 68% practitioner belief, noting it measures opinion, not effect.

unsupported_claims: The draft says the 11% increase in new reviews is a 'measurable effect' alongside the calls result, but the notes report no significance test for review volume, so the effect's reliability is unknown.
'Average ratings stayed at 4.6 in both groups' implies a before-and-after comparison. The notes give only the post-study averages (4.6 in both groups), not a change measure.
factual_concerns: 'The evidence here shows a business benefit' overstates the findings. Only the calls result is reported as statistically significant; the review-volume result has no significance reported, and the ranking result is null.

The draft describes the 0.4 result as a 'controlled study' finding but omits the 60/60 split and the 40-grid-point daily measurement design, which bear directly on how much weight the null result can carry.
missing_perspectives: The 2025 pilot (20 clinics, 0.9-position gain, no random assignment) is omitted. It is the only other ranking estimate in the notes and points in the opposite direction; it should be reported with its non-randomized caveat.
The auto repair study (80 shops, no ranking difference) is omitted. It is relevant as a cross-industry null result that bears on generalizing from dental clinics.

unsupported_claims: The draft says the cap 'took cars off the main inbound roads', but the traffic counts source says car traffic was 1.2% lower and the roads department states the counts cannot show what caused the change; no source attributes the drop to the cap.

The draft says transfers rose 'once extra trips were free' and attributes the unlinked-trip rise partly to transfers; the transfer source gives the 1.4 to 1.6 change and a causal reason, but the notes do not quantify how much of the 18.0% rise this explains.

The draft cites [8] (Regional transit comparison 2026 at regiontransit-data.example) which does not appear in the research notes; the Corwick figure is in the regiontransit.example source, so [8] is an unsupported citation.

The draft cites [3] nowhere in the text, and cites [2][4] and [5][8] for claims where the cited source for the 18% figure is the city press release, not the audit; the 18.0% unlinked figure is attributed to the audit [2] rather than the audit's own unlinked data, which is acceptable, but the city's 18% claim is never reported.

The 41% survey figure is presented as a finding about 'riders who travel more' but the survey is only of self-reported reasons among a subset, with 27% naming a new job or office return; the draft omits the second reason and implies the cap is the dominant explanation.
factual_concerns: Headline weekday figure is 9.6% in the independent audit, but the draft says 6.9%. No source in the notes gives 6.9%, so this figure appears wrong or unsourced.

The draft reports the 18.0% unlinked-trip rise without stating it is unlinked, and it is listed in the same paragraph as weekday journeys, which invites readers to conflate the two measures. The city's 18% press-release claim uses unlinked trips too and is presented by the city as weekday ridership growth; the draft does not flag this mismatch.

The draft implies the Corwick comparison (2.3% rise, without cap) isolates the cap effect; Corwick's rise was mostly attributed to office returns, and the notes give no Halden-versus-Corwick difference test. The draft should say the comparison is only suggestive.
The draft omits that 2024 weekday journeys were 2.0% below 2025, which is context for the trend and whether 2025 was already rising.
Weekend journeys rose 3.1%, which the draft omits; a smaller weekend rise than weekday rise is relevant to whether commuting or office return explains the change.

'Fare revenue fell 6.2%' is correct for March to August 2026 but the draft does not state the period, and the 4.8 million subsidy is described as covering 'the gap' without a source stating that it exactly offsets the revenue loss.
The draft's 'Among riders who travel more' omits that the survey base is riders who said they travel more, not all riders, and no response count or margin is given.
missing_perspectives: Measurement difference: the audit's journey definition (door-to-door, linked within 60 minutes) versus unlinked trips; the draft mixes these without explaining why the headline rise is 9.6% versus 18.0%.
Counter-evidence that transfers and free trips inflate unlinked counts, meaning the 18% figure overstates ridership growth in the sense that matters for demand.
Office return and labour-market changes as an alternative driver, given the Corwick comparison and the survey's 27% figure.
Cost-side and fiscal implications beyond the 4.8 million subsidy, including whether the subsidy is sustainable.
Limits of the rider survey (self-selection, recall, question wording) and the traffic counts' inability to attribute causes, which the roads department explicitly states.
suggested_revisions: Replace the 6.9% figure with 9.6% (the audited journey figure) or find a source for 6.9%.
Separate journeys (9.6%) from unlinked trips (18.0%) explicitly, and note that the city's 18% claim uses unlinked trips and is not the same measure as weekday journeys.
Remove the claim that the cap took cars off the inbound roads, or state that traffic counts fell 1.2% and their cause is unknown.
Report the survey finding with both reasons (41% fare cap, 27% new job or office return) and note the survey's limits.
Describe the Corwick result as a non-cap comparison that suggests a background rise, not a clean control, and cite the correct regional source.
Add the weekend (3.1%) and 2024 baseline (2.0%) figures for context.
Fix citation [8], which is not in the notes, and remove or correct the uncited [3] press release reference.

unsupported_claims: The draft says transfers per journey rose 'partly because' unlinked trips rose 18.0%, and that transfers rose 'once extra trips were free'; the transfer source attributes the rise to capped riders no longer paying per transfer, not to a causal link with the 18.0% unlinked-trip figure, and the notes do not show that the 18.0% rise is explained by transfers.
The draft cites [2][4] for the claim that unlinked trips rose 18.0% 'partly because' transfers rose, but the audit source [2] reports the 18.0% figure only as a fact and gives no causal explanation.

The draft attributes the 41% figure to 'riders who travel more' without noting it is a survey subgroup (riders who said they travel more), so it does not establish the share of all riders or the cause of the overall rise.

The draft implies the fare cap is the explanation for the 9.6% rise, but no cited source tests that causal link; the survey and Corwick comparison are the only relevant evidence and neither isolates the cap's effect.
The 'weekday ridership' question is answered without the weekend comparison (3.1%) or the 2024 baseline (2.0% below 2025), which bear on whether the change is cap-specific or part of a trend.
factual_concerns: The 18% city figure is presented as an unlinked-trip count, but the draft then says unlinked trips 'did rise 18.0%' citing the audit. The audit's 18.0% is for the same six months; the draft conflates the city's rounded claim with the audit's measured figure without stating the city release may be rounding the same number.

The draft presents the 9.6% (journeys) and 18.0% (unlinked trips) figures without explaining the measurement difference: the audit defines a journey as origin to destination regardless of vehicles, so 9.6% and 18% measure different things. The draft fails to make this clear, leaving the reader to think the city's 18% is an overstatement or a different event.

The Corwick comparison is described as a 'nearby city without a cap' but the draft omits that Corwick's rise was 'mostly attributed to office returns,' which weakens the inference that the cap alone drove Halden's growth; the draft's placement implies a contrast that is not supported.

'Fare revenue fell 6.2%' is accurate for March to August 2026, but the draft omits the period and the comparison basis, and does not note that falling revenue alongside rising trips is consistent with the fare cap's design (free trips after cap) rather than a separate finding.

The fare cap description omits that the cap is per day and per week and that trips after the cap are free, which the draft partly covers but the text as written does not explain how it changes per-trip cost for frequent riders.
The draft cites [1] for the cap terms and [2] for the 9.6% figure, which is correct, but the transfer claim is cited to [2][4] where [2] does not support the transfer link.
missing_perspectives: Traffic counts (car traffic down 1.2%) are omitted; the roads department says these cannot show causes, but the draft never addresses whether modal shift from cars is a plausible contributor or explicitly rules it out.
Weekend ridership (up 3.1%) is omitted; comparing weekday and weekend change helps separate commuting effects from cap effects.
The 2024 baseline (2025 was 2.0% above 2024) is omitted, so the reader cannot judge whether 2025 is an unusual comparison year.
The survey result that 27% cited a new job or office return as the main reason is omitted, though it is a direct counter-explanation to the cap.
The limitations of the survey (self-reported, subgroup of riders who said they travel more, no response rate or sample size given in notes) are not discussed.
The finance report's subsidy of 4.8 million is presented without context on whether it offsets the full revenue loss or what the net cost to the city was.
No discussion of whether the 9.6% audit estimate, which links tap-ins within 60 minutes, could be sensitive to that linking window.
suggested_revisions: Separate the two measures explicitly: state that the audit's journey-based rise is 9.6% and the unlinked-trip rise is 18.0%, define each per the audit methodology, and explain that the city's 18% refers to unlinked trips.

Remove or reword the causal claim that transfers rose 'partly because' unlinked trips rose; state only that the transfer rate rose from 1.4 to 1.6 and that the source attributes this to capped riders no longer paying per transfer.

Add the counter-evidence: Corwick (no cap) rose 2.3%, mostly attributed to office returns, and 27% of surveyed riders cited a new job or office return; state that the notes do not isolate the cap's effect.
Qualify the 41% figure as a share of surveyed riders who said they travel more, not of all riders, and note the survey's limitations.
Add weekend (+3.1%), 2024 baseline context, and the car traffic (-1.2%) result with the roads department caveat.
Note the time window for all figures (six months from 1 March 2026) and the fare revenue period (March to August 2026) so the comparisons are clearly like-for-like.

unsupported_claims: 'The shorter return window caused most of the decline [1]' is unsupported: the audit explicitly does not attribute the decline to any single cause, and no note quantifies a causal share for the window change.

The 52% wrong-size figure is described as 'of returns'; the survey covers only shoppers who returned apparel and gives wrong size as the main reason, so it is survey-based self-report rather than a share of all returns.
Citation [7] (corvane-summary.example) does not appear in the research notes; it is an unsupported or fabricated source. It is also cited for the return-window claim, which comes from [4] only.
Source [3] (FitRight customer story) is listed but never cited in the text, and its 19% claim is not addressed.
factual_concerns: The 2025 baseline is wrong: the notes say 27.1%, not 21.7%. This turns a 3.3-point decline into a misstated 2.1-point decline.

The 4.1-point May–Dec drop is presented as supporting the window change, but it is not a full-year figure and is not comparable to the 3.3-point annual decline; it is also larger than the annual drop, which the draft doesn't reconcile. The FitRight comparison (19.2% vs 25.6%) is described as 'coincided', but it is a pilot comparison of comparable orders, not an overall effect; with only 14% adoption the tool can explain only a small part of the aggregate decline. The draft states the 14% but does not draw this implication.
The FitRight 19.2% figure comes from Corvane's own evaluation, and the vendor's 19% claim covers only tool orders; the draft should not let readers conflate this with the overall rate.

Context from 2024 (26.4%) showing the 2025 rate of 27.1% was a rise and 2026 is below both; omitted.

# Corvane's online apparel returns in 2026

Corvane's audited online apparel return rate was 23.8% in 2026, down from 27.1% in 2025 [1]. The audit does not attribute the decline to a single cause.

Orders placed with the FitRight sizing tool had a 19.2% return rate, compared with 25.6% for comparable orders without it; the tool was used on 14% of online apparel orders [2]. FitRight reports a 19% return rate for orders placed with its tool [3]. In April 2026, Corvane shortened its return window from 60 to 30 days. Return rates from May to December were 4.1 percentage points lower than in the same months of 2025 [4].

Wrong size was the main reason for 52% of apparel returns [5], and each online apparel return cost an average of $11.40 to process [6].

### Sources
[1] Corvane Annual Returns Audit 2026: https://corvane-audit.example/2026  
[2] FitRight pilot evaluation: https://corvane-audit.example/fitright-pilot  
[3] FitRight customer story: Corvane: https://fitright-blog.example/corvane  
[4] Return policy change notice: https://corvane-news.example/returns-window  
[5] Shopper survey on returns: https://shopperpulse.example/corvane-2026  
[6] Cost of returns: https://corvane-audit.example/cost

unsupported_claims: 'The cap also took cars off the main inbound roads' is unsupported. The traffic counts source shows only a 1.2% fall in car traffic, and the roads department says the counts cannot show cause. The draft also does not cite the traffic counts source.
Citation [8] (regiontransit-data.example/compare) does not match any source in the notes. It is a fabricated or unverified source, and the Corwick figure is already covered by [5].

The draft implies the cap caused the ridership rise. The survey shows only that 41% of riders who say they travel more named the cap. This is not a causal estimate, and the draft omits the 27% who named a new job or office return.
factual_concerns: The weekday journey increase is stated as 6.9%, but the audit says 9.6%. This is a transposition error in the headline number.

The 18.0% unlinked-trip figure is placed right after the journeys figure without saying it is a different measure. The city press release's 18% claim, which counts unlinked trips and calls it 'ridership', is not addressed. It is listed as source [3] but never cited or critiqued.

The 41% survey figure is presented as 'among riders who travel more' without noting that this is a self-selected subset and a minority of that group, so it does not show that the cap drove most of the growth.

The transfer rise from 1.4 to 1.6 is described as 'partly' explaining the unlinked-trip rise. That is plausible, but the notes do not quantify it. Note also that the 1.4 to 1.6 rise is about 14%, which is roughly consistent with the gap between 9.6% and 18%, so the draft undersells the point that the unlinked figure is largely a counting artifact.

The Corwick comparison is mentioned but never used. The draft does not say that Halden's 9.6% minus Corwick's 2.3% leaves about 7 points as a rough upper bound on the cap's effect, and that Corwick's rise is attributed to office returns, which probably affected Halden too.
missing_perspectives: The 2024 baseline (2.0% below 2025) is omitted, so the draft gives no sense of the pre-existing trend. Its relevance is limited, but the draft should note whether a pre-cap trend existed.
Weekend journeys rose only 3.1%, which is a useful contrast. If the cap had a broad effect, the smaller weekend rise is worth discussing, and the draft leaves it out.

The audit methodology (journeys linked within 60 minutes from tap-in data) is not mentioned. The draft should note that journey figures are estimates and that the linking window may interact with the increased transfers.

The fiscal cost is underexplained. Revenue fell 6.2% while journeys rose 9.6%, and the draft does not note that revenue per journey fell. The units for the 6.50, 24 and 4.8 million figures (currency) are also missing.
The draft omits other explanations, namely office returns and a new job, which the survey names as the second most common reason (27%).
The draft does not discuss the cap design incentives, such as free trips after the cap is reached, which may shift behavior and inflate unlinked trips.
suggested_revisions: Correct the weekday journeys figure to 9.6% and cite [2].

Explicitly distinguish journeys (9.6%) from unlinked trips (18.0%) and state that the city's 18% 'ridership' claim [3] uses unlinked trips, so the audit's figure is the better measure of how many people traveled.

Remove the sentence about the cap taking cars off the roads, or replace it with: 'Car traffic on main inbound roads was 1.2% lower, but the roads department says the counts cannot show cause.' Add the traffic counts source if kept.
Delete source [8] and cite only [5] for Corwick.

Reframe the causal claim: say the cap is probably one contributor, with the evidence being the Corwick gap (about 7 points) and the survey (41% cap vs 27% job/office return), and flag that no study isolates the effect.
Add the weekend rise (3.1%) and the 2024 baseline for context, plus a note on the audit's 60-minute linking method.
Add currency units and note that revenue fell 6.2% despite higher journeys, with the subsidy covering the gap.

unsupported_claims: The draft never states that the cap caused the 9.6% rise. Still, placing the Corwick and survey figures next to it implies causation without any attribution analysis. The notes support only a partial attribution.

"partly because transfers per journey rose from 1.4 to 1.6 once extra trips were free" is the draft's own inference. The transfers source says capped riders no longer pay per transfer, which is not the same as extra trips being free in general. It also gives no breakdown of how much of the 18.0% vs 9.6% gap comes from transfers. Arithmetic: 1.6/1.4 is about +14%, which roughly reconciles with the gap, but the draft does not show this.
The draft cites the 18.0% unlinked-trip rise to [2] and the transfer figures to [2][4], but the notes do not clearly say the 18.0% is in the audit alongside the 9.6%. Verify the citation placement.
factual_concerns: The survey is reported as "Among riders who travel more, 41% named the fare cap as the main reason" without saying it is self-reported and covers only riders who said they travel more. It does not measure the share of all riders or total ridership change. It could be read as 41% of the increase, which would be wrong. It also omits that 27% named a new job or office return.
The draft gives no currency for the 6.50, 24 and 4.8 million figures; the notes do not specify one either. Flag this and avoid inventing a currency symbol.

The draft says "the city's figure of an 18% increase counts unlinked trips" but does not say that the city presents this as a weekday ridership increase caused by the cap, which makes it misleading versus journeys. The notes show the city claims the cap caused it, and the draft does not make clear the claim is overstated.

Fare revenue -6.2% and the subsidy are given without period (March-August 2026 vs 2025) and without stating that revenue fell despite higher ridership. The draft does not link this to the question or say it is not evidence of why ridership changed.
missing_perspectives: Corwick's 2.3% rise is given as a bare number. The draft should use it as a rough control: some of Halden's 9.6% may reflect office returns, which would leave roughly 7 points as a possible upper bound for the cap's effect. This should be flagged as a rough, non-causal comparison, since Corwick is a different city.
The 2024 baseline (2024 weekday journeys 2.0% below 2025) is omitted. It suggests an existing upward trend that could account for part of the year-on-year rise.

Weekend ridership rose 3.1%, which is smaller than the weekday rise. This is relevant, since the cap applies on weekends too, and the weekday-weekend gap is worth discussing as possible evidence of a cap effect or of commuting changes.
Traffic counts (-1.2% car traffic) are omitted. They could be mentioned with the roads department's caveat that causation cannot be shown, to avoid implying mode shift.
The audit methodology (journeys estimated from tap-in data linked within 60 minutes) is not stated, so readers cannot see why 9.6% and 18% differ or how uncertain the estimates are.
The survey's 27% for new job or office return, which competes with the cap as an explanation, is left out.
suggested_revisions: State a clear bottom line: weekday journeys rose 9.6% (audit), the city's 18% is unlinked trips and not comparable, and the evidence suggests the cap contributed but cannot give a precise causal share.
Define journey vs unlinked trip once, using the methodology source, and note the 60-minute linking rule.
Add the Corwick comparison as a rough benchmark, plus the 2024 baseline and the weekend +3.1%, and explicitly list competing explanations (office returns, new jobs, underlying trend).
Rewrite the survey sentence: 41% of those who said they travel more named the cap as main reason; 27% named a new job or office return; self-reported and not representative of all riders.
Add the traffic counts with the roads department caveat, and label the revenue/subsidy point as a cost of the policy, not evidence for causation.
Hedge language such as "partly because" unless the source quantifies the transfer contribution; say the transfer change plausibly explains much of the gap between 9.6% and 18.0%.
Add a short limitations note: no causal identification, different baseline years, one comparison city.

# Halden Metro ridership after the 2026 fare cap

Since 1 March 2026, Halden Metro riders pay at most 6.50 per day and 24 per week [1]. In the six months after the cap began, average weekday journeys rose 9.6% compared with the same months of 2025 [2]. Unlinked trips, which count each transfer as a separate trip, rose 18.0% over the same period [2][3].

Because capped riders no longer pay per transfer, the average number of transfers per journey rose from 1.4 to 1.6 after the cap began [4]. In Corwick, a nearby city without a cap, weekday journeys rose 2.3% over the same months [5].

Among riders who said they travel more since March 2026, 41% named the fare cap as the main reason [6]. Fare revenue from March to August 2026 was 6.2% lower than in the same months of 2025, and the city covered the gap with a 4.8 million subsidy [7]. Weekend journeys rose 3.1% over the same period [8].

# Review replies and map-pack rankings for Brennick County dental clinics

In a controlled study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics in the first half of 2026, clinics randomly assigned to reply to every review moved up 0.4 map-pack positions relative to the others, a difference that was not statistically significant [1][2].

An agency's claim of a 3-position gain comes from 9 clients of its own, with no comparison group [3]. Replying did have measurable effects elsewhere: clinics that replied received 7% more calls from their listings and collected 11% more new reviews, while average ratings stayed at 4.6 in both groups [4][5][6].
